At 03:05:13.493 the postgres container logged 'FATAL: terminating connection due to administrator command', and from 03:05:14.023 to 03:05:30.391 every application connection was rejected with 'FATAL: password authentication failed for user "otelu"' (pg_hba.conf line 128, scram-sha-256) (981e1e6c-8ac1-4f13-bc13-64b42bb30ecc-t0:22811573-5cd1-4c1c-bdfc-eebd56dd533c, e3625bfe-8de2-43fe-b40c-0bacf91c59d2-t1:b7625681-526d-4cc8-a4d2-66c9621c46f5). Database credentials are supplied differently per client: product-catalog reads DB_CONNECTION_STRING from Secret 'product-catalog-db-conn' (key DB_CONNECTION_STRING), while product-reviews and accounting carry DB_CONNECTION_STRING inline in their pod templates (values redacted), and product-catalog's pod template image digest and env were unchanged by its rollout.

Most likely mechanism: the password stored for role 'otelu' in the running PostgreSQL instance of Deployment astronomy-shop/postgresql was changed by an administrative action at about 03:05:13Z — the 'terminating connection due to administrator command' at 03:05:13.493 immediately followed by SCRAM 'password authentication failed' for otelu — so clients were rejected regardless of the password they held, including the never-restarted product-reviews pod.

Rejected: a flagd feature-flag fault (for example productCatalogFailure) causing the product failures. Every fault flag in flagd-config is 'off', and the failures carry exact PostgreSQL authentication error text rather than the flag-driven failure mode.

Rejected: a postgres crash, eviction, OOM or restart losing the role. Rejected: a general cluster or network outage. Service postgresql has exactly one healthy endpoint, the failure is an authentication rejection rather than a refused connection, all deployments are fully available with 0 pod restarts, and cart/valkey calls in the same traces succeed.

PostgreSQL shows no resource or process fault of its own: initdb and init.sql completed successfully, the pod is Running and ready with 0 restarts and no unhealthy postgres event, and the postgres readiness probe never failed in the events — only SCRAM authentication is failing, which points at a credential mismatch rather than a broken database workload.

Realign the otelu credential in one step: read the value the clients use (Secret product-catalog-db-conn and the inline DB_CONNECTION_STRING of product-reviews and accounting) and set the database to the same value with ALTER ROLE otelu PASSWORD ..., because the entrypoint init.sql is only executed on an empty data directory and can no longer change the live role.

Further restarts of product-catalog, product-reviews or accounting are not indicated: after the 03:05:05–03:05:12 rollouts their new pods still failed while the pod template image digest and secret reference were unchanged, so the rollout is not the fault.

Audit who wrote postgresql-init (kubectl-patch 03:05:09Z) and the three deployments (kubectl-set/OpenAPI-Generator 03:05:05–03:05:12Z), and who connected to PostgreSQL as an administrator at 03:05:13Z, since that actor and the exact altered field are outside the observable evidence of this Run.

view.cannot_prove: Objects are the cluster's state when the query ran, not during the incident window: they cannot prove what was true earlier, and an object missing now may have existed then. Events cover only their own timestamps inside the window; an event that is not returned is unknown, not proof nothing happened (events expire and timestamps are often null). A jq result is what the expression selected, not a full picture of the kind. When the API server returns zero objects of a kind other than events (every page read), the result is ok with total_items_processed 0: it proves only that there were no objects matching this kind, namespace and selectors at query time, not that none existed during the incident. Zero events, or a list your filter reduced to nothing, stays no_data. metadata.managedFieldsSummary gives each manager's last write time only: it is not a full change history (earlier writes by the same manager are gone) and it does not say which fields that write changed.

view.cannot_prove: A line that is not returned is unknown, not proof that nothing was logged: only limit lines are shown (the newest), and retention, ingest delay, the label selector and line filters can leave gaps. The timestamp is when the line was ingested or parsed, not necessarily when the event happened. A metric query counts only lines inside the query window.
view.incomplete_reason: limit: 100 lines were returned, the limit; older lines in the window were not returned (Loki reports no total). Narrow the selector or line filters, shorten the window, or count with count_over_time

view.cannot_prove: Objects are the cluster's state when the query ran, not during the incident window: they cannot prove what was true earlier, and an object missing now may have existed then. Events cover only their own timestamps inside the window; an event that is not returned is unknown, not proof nothing happened (events expire and timestamps are often null). A jq result is what the expression selected, not a full picture of the kind. When the API server returns zero objects of a kind other than events (every page read), the result is ok with total_items_processed 0: it proves only that there were no objects matching this kind, namespace and selectors at query time, not that none existed during the incident. Zero events, or a list your filter reduced to nothing, stays no_data. metadata.managedFieldsSummary gives each manager's last write time only: it is not a full change history (earlier writes by the same manager are gone) and it does not say which fields that write changed.
